title: How to Keep Going When God Feels Distant
excerpt: The dry season is not a sign you have failed. It is a normal part of following God, and almost everyone who has gone deep with him has walked through it.
body:
There is a season that comes to nearly everyone who follows God for any length of time, and almost no one warns you about it. The prayers that once felt warm go flat. The Bible reads like a phone book. Worship that used to move you leaves you cold. And God, who seemed near, seems to have stepped behind a wall. Nothing dramatic happened. He simply went quiet, and you are left going through motions that no longer feel like anything.

The first thing to know is that you are not alone and you have not failed. This is so common in the history of faith that the church gave it names. The dark night of the soul. The desert. The wilderness. David wrote, how long, O Lord, will you forget me forever. The desert fathers expected it. Even Jesus on the cross cried, my God, why have you forsaken me. If the absence of feeling were proof of God's absence, the most faithful people who ever lived were the most abandoned. They were not. Neither are you.

## Do not trust your feelings as a verdict

The great lie of the dry season is that the absence of feeling means the absence of God. It does not. Feelings are real, but they are weather, not climate. They report your internal state, not the state of reality. God promised never to leave you, and that promise does not expire on the days you cannot feel it. The sun does not go out when a cloud covers it. Your job in the dry season is to keep believing what God said over what your feelings report.

This is faith doing its actual work. Anyone can trust God when the feelings are flowing. Trusting him when you feel nothing, on the strength of his word alone, is faith of a deeper kind, the kind that only grows in the desert.

## Keep the practices anyway

The instinct in dryness is to stop. Why pray, why read, why gather, when none of it does anything? But this is exactly backward. The dry season is when the disciplines matter most, precisely because you are no longer being carried by feeling and must walk on commitment instead.

Keep showing up. Pray the prayers even when they feel empty. Read the word even when it seems dead. Go to church even when you would rather not. You are not faking. You are remaining faithful in the dark, which is worth more than all your faithfulness in the light. The farmer does not abandon the field in the dormant season. He tends it, trusting the spring he cannot yet see.

## Examine, but do not assume the worst

Sometimes dryness has a cause worth finding, an unconfessed sin, a slow drift, a bitterness you have nursed. So it is worth a gentle, honest look. Ask God to show you if something stands between you. But do not turn this into a frantic hunt for the secret failure that explains everything. Most dry seasons are not punishment. They are simply the desert that God leads his people through, the same way he led Israel, not because they had failed but because the desert was where they would learn to depend on him alone.

## Lean on the body of Christ

The dry season tempts you to withdraw, to hide your struggle, to drop out quietly. Do the opposite. Tell someone. Find a friend or a pastor and say plainly, God feels far away and I do not know why. You will almost certainly find they have been there too. And let the faith of others carry you when yours feels thin. This is part of why the church exists, so that when one member's lamp gutters, the others keep the room lit. You do not have to generate your own light right now. You only have to stay in the room.

## Let the desert do its work

The dry season is not wasted. It is doing something the green seasons cannot. It is teaching you to love God for himself and not for the feelings he gives, to follow him for who he is and not for the warmth of the experience. It is burning off the part of your faith that was really just emotional reward, and leaving behind something harder and truer. Many who have walked through it say afterward that the desert, though they hated it, was where their faith finally grew up.

## When it is more than dryness

Name this clearly. Spiritual dryness and clinical depression can feel almost identical from the inside, and they are not the same thing. If, along with the spiritual flatness, you have lost interest in everything, cannot sleep or sleep too much, feel hopeless for weeks, or have any thought of harming yourself, that is depression, and it needs a doctor, not just more prayer. Please reach out, to a physician, a counselor, a crisis line. There is no faithlessness in it. God heals through these means too, and your life is precious to him.

## This week

Do not wait to feel like it. Keep one simple practice every day this week, five minutes of prayer or one psalm, whether or not anything happens. Then tell one trusted person the plain truth, that God feels distant right now. Do not try to fix the feeling. Just stay faithful in the dark and let someone walk with you.

The sun has not gone out. You are simply in the part of the path where you walk by his word and not by the warmth. Keep walking. The desert ends.
